paragraphs: Personalized federated learning lets participants collaborate while keeping their raw data private and maintaining individual models. The central question here is how much each participant should learn from everyone else. The paper makes those collaboration weights learnable: each participant minimizes a weighted combination of the participants’ empirical losses, rather than using weights chosen in advance.

The authors estimate the weights through kernel mean embeddings, representations of data distributions that make statistical relationships between participants accessible. Tools from multi-task averaging then determine how to combine information across sources. This produces an adaptive procedure that needs no prior description of data heterogeneity and can move between shared global learning and more independent local learning.

Reformulating the problem as high-dimensional mean estimation yields finite-sample guarantees for local excess risk across a broad distribution class. These guarantees quantify the statistical benefits of collaboration. A practical version uses random Fourier features to trade communication cost against statistical efficiency, and numerical experiments support the theoretical results.
icml-2026-adaptive-personalized-federate.tldr: Learned collaboration weights adapt personalized federated learning to participants’ data differences, with statistical guarantees and a communication-efficiency trade-off.

paragraphs: Constrained online optimization requires making decisions repeatedly while managing both prediction or decision loss and violations of constraints. CLASP addresses these objectives together by penalizing squared violations. Its two variants, CLASP-I and CLASP-F, allow the fixed decision set and changing constraints to be handled jointly or separately. Separating them can simplify implementation when projection onto the fixed set is easy.

The analysis uses cutter operators and their contraction properties to control the learning process. For convex losses, both variants have regret bounded by O(T raised to max(beta, 1−beta)) and cumulative squared penalty bounded by O(T raised to 1−beta), for any beta between zero and one. The parameter therefore determines the theoretical balance between the two bounds as the number of rounds grows.

For strongly convex problems, the paper establishes logarithmic bounds on both regret and cumulative squared penalty, presenting these simultaneous guarantees as a first. The distinction matters: stronger curvature assumptions support substantially slower growth of both quantities than the general convex guarantees.
icml-2026-clasp-online-learning-algorith.tldr: CLASP controls online loss and squared constraint violations, achieving logarithmic bounds for both under strong convexity.

paragraphs: A robot policy must express its decisions in some action representation, and that choice influences how readily it learns from demonstrations. This paper studies action design as a substantive part of policy learning. It asks how different representations affect both the learning problem and the stability of the resulting robot control, addressing choices often inherited from convention or selected heuristically.

The study organizes action choices along temporal and spatial axes. It compares absolute targets with delta actions, which describe changes, and joint-space commands with task-space commands. The evidence comes from more than 13,000 physical robot rollouts on a bimanual platform and evaluations of over 500 trained models across four scenarios.

The results suggest that properly designing a policy to predict delta actions consistently improves performance in the study. Spatial representations show complementary strengths: joint-space actions favor control stability, while task-space actions favor generalization. These findings make action representation a practical design consideration alongside training data and model capacity, while preserving the empirical nature of the conclusions.
icml-2026-demystifying-action-space-desi.tldr: A large robot study finds benefits from properly designed delta actions and complementary stability and generalization strengths across spatial representations.

paragraphs: This paper connects dropout scheduling to a theory of how signals propagate through neural networks near the edge of chaos. Its practical finding is that front-loaded dropout schedules reduce test loss by 18–35% relative to constant dropout in the studied multilayer perceptrons and Vision Transformers, at a fixed budget. Accuracy improvements appear as a consistent secondary effect.

The theory treats dropout as a disturbance to critical signal propagation. Dropout shifts the state of perfect alignment between signals, making the depth over which information propagates finite even at critical initialization. The authors derive scaling laws for correlation decay and distinguish two classes of behavior: networks with smooth activations and networks with kinked, ReLU-like activations.

That distinction comes from the mathematical behavior of the correlation map near perfect alignment, producing different critical exponents. The framework also yields saturated dropout profiles under a fixed budget, while a regularization-reach argument selects front-loaded schedules. The authors discuss extensions toward convolutional and residual architectures through a shared Gaussian-kernel structure.
icml-2026-dropout-universality-scaling-l.tldr: A signal-propagation theory motivates front-loaded dropout schedules that lower test loss by 18–35% in the reported fixed-budget experiments.

paragraphs: Extending a pretrained video generator to produce long sequences requires more than repeatedly producing additional frames. Frame-level autoregressive methods can continue indefinitely with constant memory, but their inference conditions differ from training, and consistency becomes difficult to maintain over time. MIGA addresses these problems within train-free long-video generation, aiming to make better use of existing foundation models.

Its first component is a two-stage alignment mechanism. This reduces the excessive spread of noise levels presented to the model, narrowing the training–inference gap. The second component combines two forms of consistency enhancement. Self-reflection corrects early frames that still contain substantial noise, while long-range guidance uses later, less noisy frames with broad coverage to steer generation.

These components address different sources of difficulty: alignment improves the conditions under which the pretrained model operates, while the paired guidance mechanisms improve temporal consistency. Experiments on VBench and NarrLV report state-of-the-art performance for MIGA. The contribution concerns the quality and coherence of continued generation; the ability to keep producing frames alone does not establish long-term consistency.
icml-2026-enhancing-train-free-infinite-.tldr: MIGA improves train-free long-video generation by aligning noise conditions and combining early-frame correction with long-range guidance.

paragraphs: Reasoning can become harder because a relation requires several entities to be considered together, even when the input contains no additional entities overall. This paper isolates that difficulty using relational complexity: the minimum number of independent entities or operands that must be bound simultaneously to apply a relation. The goal is to distinguish this demand from input length, vocabulary, or presentation.

The authors introduce REL, a generative benchmark framework covering algebra, chemistry, and biology. Within each domain, it varies relational complexity to examine how models handle increasingly demanding combinations. Evaluations of frontier language models show a consistent, monotonic decline in performance as complexity increases, including when the total number of entities remains fixed.

The observed failure persists with additional test-time computation and in-context examples. This suggests that the difficulty is associated with the number of entities that must be related simultaneously, rather than simply too few reasoning steps or examples. REL therefore identifies a specific regime of reasoning weakness and provides a more targeted way to evaluate it.
icml-2026-evaluating-relational-reasonin.tldr: REL finds that language-model performance declines as more entities must be related simultaneously, even with fixed entity counts and added inference support.

paragraphs: Functional ANOVA explains predictions by separating individual feature effects from interactions among features. Under feature independence, this decomposition is well established and closely connected to SHAP explanations. Dependence between inputs complicates the picture: the absence of a general explicit expression has led practitioners to use costly sampling approximations. This paper resolves that obstacle for categorical inputs.

The authors connect functional analysis with an extension of discrete Fourier analysis to derive a closed-form decomposition. Within the categorical setting, it accommodates arbitrary dependence structures without imposing an independence assumption. It also covers non-rectangular support, meaning the distribution need not include every combination of possible feature values. The classical independent-feature case emerges within the same formulation.

The paper describes the resulting computation as highly efficient. It also uses the established ANOVA–SHAP relationship under independence to construct a natural generalization of SHAP values for categorical inputs more broadly. The contribution makes dependence part of the explanation framework itself, extending exact effect and interaction analysis beyond the independent setting.
icml-2026-exact-functional-anova-decompo.tldr: A closed-form functional ANOVA decomposition handles arbitrarily dependent categorical inputs and supports a natural generalization of SHAP values.

paragraphs: GenCircuit-RL trains language models to design genetic circuits by producing code. The models generate Python using PySBOL to represent circuits in the standardized SBOL format. This turns an expert-intensive biological design task into a structured generation problem in which proposed designs can receive feedback at several levels of correctness.

The reinforcement-learning rewards use five verification levels, ranging from whether code executes to whether circuit structure and functional behavior are correct. This hierarchy supplies denser feedback than a single final success signal. Multiplicative dependencies between levels are used to prevent reward hacking. A four-stage curriculum gradually shifts training emphasis from producing basic working code toward satisfying functional requirements.

The accompanying SynBio-Reason benchmark contains approximately 4,753 circuits across six canonical circuit types and nine tasks, including repair and design from scratch. Holding out biological parts enables evaluation on unfamiliar components. The reported results show compact models producing functionally correct circuits, generalizing to novel parts, and rediscovering canonical designs, supporting the combination of hierarchical verification and progressive training.
icml-2026-gencircuit-rl-reinforcement-le.tldr: GenCircuit-RL combines layered verification rewards and curriculum learning to train compact language models for genetic-circuit code generation.

paragraphs: Post-hoc text watermarking rewrites an existing document while inserting a statistical signal that can later be detected. This paper investigates that approach for copyright protection and for detecting document use in training or retrieval-augmented generation. Because rewriting happens after the original text exists, the system has additional choices about how to generate candidates and detect their watermarks.

The study examines how computation affects the balance between preserving text quality and making the watermark detectable. It considers larger rewriting models, beam search, multiple candidate generations, and entropy filtering during detection. Under nucleus sampling, the simple Gumbel-max watermark performs better than more recent alternatives and provides strong detectability while preserving meaning in open-ended material such as books.

Most evaluated methods benefit substantially from beam search, while smaller models unexpectedly outperform larger ones in the study. The approach struggles with verifiable text such as code. The findings therefore support post-hoc watermarking for some kinds of text while showing that model size and rewriting flexibility do not automatically produce better results.
icml-2026-how-good-is-post-hoc-watermark.tldr: Rephrasing-based watermarking shows strong results on open-ended text, but struggles with code and does not consistently benefit from larger models.

paragraphs: Mixup creates additional training examples by interpolating between existing examples. Although the idea has worked in other data domains, applying it to graphs raises questions about what a meaningful interpolation should look like. This paper independently evaluates existing graph mixup methods using a unified, established protocol for graph classification.

Under that protocol, none of the evaluated state-of-the-art methods produces a statistically significant improvement over training without mixup. This differs from previously reported results and makes the shared evaluation procedure central to the contribution. The finding concerns the tested methods and settings; it does not establish that every possible graph augmentation strategy must fail.

The authors also examine the generated graphs as interpolations. Many methods interpolate poorly, and high interpolation error is associated with performance degradation in their analysis. Yet methods with good interpolation properties still do not improve performance. These observations separate two questions that can otherwise be conflated: whether an augmentation meaningfully interpolates and whether those interpolations actually help graph classification.
icml-2026-is-graph-mixup-beneficial-inve.tldr: A unified evaluation finds no statistically significant gains from tested graph mixup methods, even when their interpolation quality is good.

paragraphs: Spectral graph methods describe signals using the graph Fourier transform, but computing its eigenbasis is expensive and its representations lack vertex-level locality. Common alternatives rely on local message passing or polynomial filters, which limit their ability to capture distant relationships. L2G-Net introduces a construction that connects subgraph processing to a global spectral representation.

The mathematical core is an exact factorization of the graph Fourier transform into operators on subgraphs, combined through a sequence of Cauchy matrices. The resulting network processes spectral information locally and then joins it using these structured matrices. Construction avoids a full eigendecomposition, with complexity quadratic in the number of nodes and scaled by the largest cut between subgraphs.

Experiments emphasize long-range dependencies on large graphs. They show operation at scales beyond the standard graph Fourier transform and performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods using orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters. The contribution is therefore an exact local-to-global spectral construction with demonstrated scaling benefits, rather than solely another local approximation.
icml-2026-l2g-net-local-to-global-spectr.tldr: L2G-Net factors the graph Fourier transform through subgraphs to model long-range structure with fewer parameters and improved practical scalability.

paragraphs: World models let agents learn and plan through imagined interactions, but their internal representations can preserve many details irrelevant to control. This paper asks how an agent can instead learn a compact representation that retains what it needs for decision making. The approach connects data collection and representation learning in a closed loop.

On the exploration side, the agent actively probes the environment to expose hidden factors relevant to its tasks. An adaptive curriculum guides this collection of informative interaction sequences. On the modeling side, structured learning distills those observations into compact latent states. The two components work together: informative experience supplies the material from which the world model extracts useful structure.

Empirically, the resulting representations capture all control-relevant factors in the studied settings. Policies built on them improve sample efficiency and generalization on continuous-control and robotic-manipulation benchmarks. Reported generalization includes transfer across skills, combinations of objects and skills, and previously unseen tasks. The findings support jointly designing exploration and representation learning to focus the model on decision-relevant information.
icml-2026-learning-task-sufficient-world.tldr: Active exploration and structured world-model learning jointly produce compact control-relevant representations that improve empirical efficiency and generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies when a graph neural network can learn to execute a graph algorithm exactly. Its guarantees apply under bounded-degree and finite-precision constraints. These conditions define the setting of the result, so the claim concerns exact learnability within that setting rather than unrestricted algorithm learning on arbitrary graphs.

The method separates learning local behavior from running the full algorithm. First, an ensemble of multilayer perceptrons learns the instructions carried out by an individual node. At inference, that trained ensemble becomes the update function of a graph neural network. The authors use Neural Tangent Kernel theory to show that the local instructions can be learned from a small training set.

The resulting graph algorithm executes without error with high probability under the stated constraints. The analysis establishes learnability for the LOCAL model of distributed computation and positive results for message flooding, breadth-first search, depth-first search, and Bellman-Ford. Its significance is a rigorous connection between learning local rules and correctly composing them into complete graph computations.
icml-2026-learning-to-execute-graph-algo.tldr: Under bounded-degree and finite-precision constraints, learned local update rules enable exact graph-algorithm execution with high probability.

paragraphs: Running several agent teams in parallel can explore different routes to a solution, but it also duplicates work. Teams may independently solve similar subproblems or repeat analogous tool-driven steps. Learning to Share addresses this computational overlap by allowing teams to reuse selected intermediate results through a common memory bank.

The central component is a lightweight controller that decides which intermediate steps should enter shared memory. It is trained with stepwise reinforcement learning and usage-aware credit assignment, so its learning signal reflects information’s usefulness across parallel executions. Selective admission also controls context growth: the mechanism seeks valuable shared information rather than indiscriminately accumulating every step.

Experiments on AssistantBench and GAIA show significantly lower overall runtime while matching or improving task performance relative to parallel systems without memory. The results support learned memory admission as a way to preserve the benefits of multiple reasoning trajectories while reducing repeated computation. The contribution centers on deciding what deserves to be shared, alongside making cross-team reuse possible.
icml-2026-learning-to-share-selective-me.tldr: Learning to Share trains a selective memory controller that reduces parallel-agent runtime while matching or improving benchmark task performance.

paragraphs: A video question-answering system can give a correct answer while identifying the wrong supporting moment. LINGUA targets this grounding gap by maintaining an explicit language-based belief state. It combines event-driven perception with typed memories for episode narratives, semantic affordances, and procedural scripts, giving the agent organized information to reason over.

The system uses Belief-Action-Verification loops with checks on postconditions and timing, alongside reflection and contrastive refinement. Bayesian reliability tracking supports continued learning through memory without gradient updates. Its perception stage retains 8–12% of frames while preserving 94% of question-relevant events, linking selective observation to reduced processing.

Built on quantized Gemma3-4B, LINGUA outperforms strong baselines across five benchmarks and runs 2.6 times faster than dense-frame methods. It reaches 82.4% on NExT-QA and 42.3% on NExT-GQA’s measure combining correct answers with temporal localization at IoU of at least 0.5. Across 100 videos, accuracy increases from 45.2% on the first ten to 61.8% on the last ten without reported catastrophic forgetting.
icml-2026-lingua-bridging-the-grounding-.tldr: LINGUA uses structured memory and explicit verification to improve video answers, temporal grounding, and online adaptation without gradient updates.

paragraphs: Mantis is a transformer-based foundation model designed for time-series classification, a task the paper identifies as less explored than forecasting. Its pretraining uses exclusively synthetic data and self-supervised contrastive learning. The work examines how that training approach, together with representation design, can support classification across diverse application domains.

A central architectural contribution is a new token generator unit. The paper finds that effective tokenization is critical to realizing the transformer’s potential for this task. It also introduces a test-time methodology that uses representations from intermediate layers, self-ensembling, and fusion of embeddings from different models. These components broaden the information used when making classification decisions.

Experiments across four diverse dataset collections report a new state of the art and improvements over existing foundation models. The enhanced test-time approach also bridges the performance gap with strong specialized methods. The findings connect performance to both the representation learned during synthetic pretraining and the way model representations are combined at evaluation time.
icml-2026-mantis-lightweight-foundation-.tldr: Mantis combines synthetic contrastive pretraining, tailored tokenization, and enhanced test-time representations for strong time-series classification.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts systems can reduce forgetting as new tasks arrive, but their organization creates a tension. A shared parameter space can become a bottleneck across many tasks, while fully independent experts require a separate mechanism to identify the task. This paper removes the inter-task shared parameter space and the explicit task-ID predictor, using dynamic communication among experts instead.

A multimodal foundation model such as CLIP supplies expert priors through its open-set capabilities. These priors strengthen task-specific representations and guide experts in learning calibrated inter-task posteriors. Multivariate Gaussian models over those posteriors encourage experts to specialize in complementary ways. Knowledge sharing therefore occurs through the prior-conditioned interaction among experts.

The authors introduce benchmarks intended to reflect realistic continual-learning scenarios. Their strategy consistently outperforms existing methods across the evaluated settings without reference datasets or replay memory. The findings support a form of expert collaboration that shares useful knowledge while avoiding the particular shared-parameter bottleneck identified in the paper.
icml-2026-mixing-expertise-with-confiden.tldr: Prior-guided expert communication improves evaluated multimodal continual learning without an inter-task shared parameter space, explicit task router, or replay memory.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often spend substantial resources moving data through irregular memory accesses. Complex layers can also create intermediate values for individual edges, increasing traffic and memory use. This paper organizes common layers into three computational families—sparse matrix multiplication, reductions, and attention—and develops GPU implementations around their data-movement requirements.

The approach reduces memory traffic and improves locality through family-specific kernels. Graph reordering helps differently depending on the mapping of work: neighbor-parallel kernels benefit more consistently than feature-parallel ones. For sparse-matrix-based layers, properly cached cuSPARSE outperforms evaluated custom baselines in most evaluations, showing that implementation choices matter alongside new kernel designs.

Reported median speedups are 1.6 times for Graph Transformer, 2.0 times for GATv2, and 2.6 times for degree-aware reductions. GATv2 peak memory falls by a median factor of six, with a maximum reduction of 76 times. Block-sparse Tensor Core variants reach up to 7.3 times speedup on locally dense graphs. The released implementations are designed as drop-in replacements.
icml-2026-on-efficient-scaling-of-gnns-v.tldr: GPU implementations tailored to graph-layer memory access deliver substantial measured speed and memory improvements, with benefits depending on kernel and graph structure.

paragraphs: This paper examines how network architecture shapes the kinds of data structure a score-based generative model preferentially captures. It focuses on anisotropy: differences in behavior across directions. The question is whether those directional preferences can explain model behavior and offer information about generalization before training begins.

The authors introduce Score Anisotropy Directions, or SADs, to describe these architecture-dependent preferences. Their analysis suggests that SADs act as adaptive bases aligned with the geometry of the network’s outputs. In this account, the architecture supplies a directional organization that helps characterize what the model is predisposed to represent. This offers a principled route toward predicting generalization in advance.

Experiments use both synthetic data and standard image benchmarks. SADs capture fine-grained differences in model behavior and correlate with downstream performance measured using Wasserstein metrics. Those results support SADs as an explanatory and predictive diagnostic. The evidence is a measured relationship between architectural directions and performance, while the adaptive-basis interpretation remains framed as a suggestion of the analysis.
icml-2026-on-the-anisotropy-of-score-bas.tldr: Score Anisotropy Directions characterize architectural biases in score models and correlate with their downstream generative performance.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process posterior sampling is used for continuous-control decisions under uncertainty, but its theoretical guarantees have had important gaps. Earlier regret analyses either grew too quickly, imposed strong smoothness conditions, or did not properly handle unbounded state spaces. This paper develops an analysis that addresses those issues without assuming the entire space of possible states is bounded.

The key step distinguishes possible states from states the algorithm actually visits. A recursive application of the Borell–Tsirelson–Ibragimov–Sudakov inequality shows that the visited states remain inside a ball of near-constant radius with high probability. The authors then apply chaining to control regret under weak smoothness conditions.

The main Bayesian regret bound has order H times the square root of gamma_T times T, up to logarithmic factors. Here H is the horizon, T counts time steps, and gamma_T is expected information gain. The result ties learning difficulty to information acquisition while accommodating an unbounded state space, and supplies tools for analyzing posterior sampling in more complex settings.
icml-2026-posterior-sampling-reinforceme.tldr: A high-probability bound on visited states enables sharper Bayesian regret guarantees for Gaussian-process posterior sampling in unbounded state spaces.

paragraphs: Large sparse linear systems are a computational bottleneck in scientific computing and graph analysis. Algebraic multigrid offers linear scaling, but its practical performance depends on coarse-grid operators that must balance sparsity with effective convergence. Making those operators sparse can compromise stability or solver performance. RAPNet learns to construct sparse, robust coarse operators directly from the algebraic system.

The framework uses a graph neural network with a level-wise training strategy. This allows learning on small subgraphs and generalization to domains containing millions of nodes, addressing scaling bottlenecks in earlier neural multigrid approaches. The learned component runs only during solver setup, so the solve phase retains its favorable computational properties.

Across evaluated partial-differential-equation discretizations and graph Laplacians, RAPNet outperforms classical non-Galerkin baselines. The paper identifies particular value for tasks involving repeated queries, including eigenproblems, time-dependent simulations, and inverse or design problems. Its central contribution is to improve the operators prepared for the solver while keeping neural execution out of the subsequent solve phase.
icml-2026-rapnet-accelerating-algebraic-.tldr: RAPNet learns sparse multigrid coarse operators during setup, improving evaluated solver performance and scaling from small training subgraphs to million-node domains.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks deployed on incomplete data need evaluations that reveal meaningful differences in robustness. This paper argues that common missing-feature tests are often too benign. They frequently use sparse, high-dimensional features and remove values completely at random, conditions that can hide the difficulties encountered with more informative features and structured missingness.

The authors prove that high feature sparsity substantially limits the information lost through missingness. Consequently, many models can appear robust, making comparisons less informative. To address this, they introduce one synthetic and three real-world datasets with dense, semantically meaningful features. They also design protocols that extend beyond completely random removal.

A theoretical treatment makes assumptions about the missingness process explicit and examines their consequences for different methods. Guided by that analysis, a simple baseline adapted to graphs performs competitively with specialized architectures across diverse datasets and missingness regimes. The contribution therefore combines a critique of existing evidence, more demanding evaluations, and a practical baseline whose strength becomes visible under broader testing.
icml-2026-rethinking-gnns-and-missing-fe.tldr: More realistic missing-feature evaluations expose weaknesses in common graph benchmarks and show a simple adapted baseline competing with specialized methods.

paragraphs: Sign-based optimizers can deliver strong performance with a small memory footprint, but fixed-magnitude updates discard gradient-size information. That can become problematic near convergence, particularly when parameters behave differently: updates may continue oscillating instead of settling. SoftSignum addresses this issue by replacing the hard sign operation with a smooth, temperature-controlled transformation.

The transformation allows individual parameters to move between sign-like updates and magnitude-sensitive steps resembling stochastic gradient descent. An adaptive schedule based on quantiles controls the temperature. The authors extend the same principle to matrix-valued optimization in SoftMuon, making smooth relaxation applicable beyond individual scalar updates.

The paper also develops a general geometry-relaxation framework using strongly convex regularizers and Fenchel conjugates, and proves convergence in a stochastic non-convex setting. Experiments across diverse deep-learning tasks, including language-model pretraining, show consistent improvements over the evaluated hard-sign counterparts and AdamW. Together, the analysis and experiments support restoring sensitivity to gradient magnitude as a way to handle parameter heterogeneity more effectively.
icml-2026-softsign-smooth-sign-in-your-o.tldr: SoftSignum and SoftMuon smooth fixed-magnitude optimizer updates, improving reported training results while supporting stochastic non-convex convergence analysis.

paragraphs: Positional encodings give graph neural networks additional information about graph structure. Complete spectral and random-walk encodings have equivalent theoretical expressive power, but the complete versions require cubic time and space in the number of nodes. Practical systems therefore retain only a subset, such as the first few eigenspaces or adjacency-matrix powers.

This paper investigates what truncation does to those expressivity guarantees. It shows that several encoding families become fundamentally different once truncated, so equivalence of their complete forms does not transfer automatically to practical versions. In particular, truncated spectral encodings are no longer stronger than the 1-WL test. The analysis of k-harmonic distances also reveals differences among closely related spectral encodings.

Experiments on real-world datasets find that mixing truncated encoding families is preferable to using a single family. The theoretical and empirical findings point in the same practical direction: the retained portion of an encoding matters, and families that look interchangeable in their complete mathematical form can supply different structural information after truncation.
icml-2026-understanding-truncated-positi.tldr: Truncation breaks expressivity equivalences between graph positional encodings, and experiments favor combining truncated families.

paragraphs: Directed graphs encode relationships whose orientation matters, but adapting undirected graph networks can worsen oversmoothing and gradient problems. Unitary graph convolutions already offer guarantees against representational collapse, yet the existing UniConv formulation cannot incorporate edge direction or features. Dune extends this approach to include both while retaining its protective guarantees.

Dune keeps gradient norms bounded at any depth and is proved to avoid the exponential oversmoothing affecting existing directed networks. Its unitary operator can also be placed inside hybrid graph-transformer architectures. There, wavelike propagation provides positional information and reduces the importance of separate random-walk or Laplacian encodings.

The empirical study reports state-of-the-art performance on 12 directed-graph benchmarks, trainability beyond 100 layers, and improvements of up to 18 percentage points over strong baselines. These findings support using depth in directed graph models without the same collapse behavior. The theoretical guarantees concern stability and oversmoothing, while the benchmark results establish the reported task-performance benefits.
icml-2026-unitary-convolutions-for-messa.tldr: Dune extends unitary graph convolutions to directed edges and edge features, combining stability guarantees with strong results beyond 100 layers.
